source.title: When Is Rank-1 Steering Cheap? Geometry, Granularity, and Budgeted Search
source.authors: J. Robertson; Jia-Ning Zhu; Haris Vikalo; Zhang-Yang Wang

record.tranche_reason: The study measures concept-level activation-direction geometry and rank-1 steering in language models, not individual-neuron responses or polysemanticity as defined by any claim version.
record.gate_note: The paper's findings concern directional heterogeneity across contrastive contexts and steering-vector performance, not whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs. These related but different measurements are recorded under fits_no_version. Steering-search results and cited prior-work results are not rows for the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study analyses residual-stream contrastive steering directions and rank-1 steering cost across concepts in LLMs. It never measures individual neurons or whether they respond to unrelated inputs. It mentions SAEs and Neuronpedia only in passing, as related work and as a source of concept ideas, so it neither tests nor uses the polysemanticity claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors argue that the main obstacle to rank-1 steering is optimization cost, not representational feasibility. Prompt-boundary alignment guides layer search, cutting T95 by 39.8%. Granularity predicts both the steering ceiling and search cost. Cross-context rotation is a persistent source of difficulty, while prompt-pair heterogeneity, magnitude outliers and representational fragmentation are removable.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops and evaluates a geometry-guided rank-1 steering workflow; it does not apply the original neuron-polysemanticity methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that concept granularity and steering behavior vary across concepts and models; it also distinguishes prompt-boundary from response-averaged activation geometry.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher concept granularity (cross-question rotation of contrastive directions) is associated with lower best-found rank-1 steering utility and more search trials needed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concept directions in LLM residual streams rotate across input contexts, and this heterogeneity limits single-vector steering.

fits_no_version.finding: Question and interaction effects each account for about 42% of directional variance in contrastive activations; prompt effects account for 16%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Contrastive concept directions are substantially context-dependent rather than a single global direction.

record.problems: The evidence concerns concept-level activation directions rather than neurons. Experiments cover 20 concepts and three model families; steering quality is evaluated with an LLM judge, and the paper reports that judges differ in absolute score calibration.
record.rows_left_out: Steering-search and construction-remedy outcomes in Sections 3–6 and Appendices J.1–J.4 were left out because they measure intervention performance, not neuron-level polysemanticity. Cited results from prior work were also excluded.
record.verdict_notes: The relation was changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only' because polysemanticity and superposition are never discussed; SAE work appears only as a citation. None of the results bear on neuron-level polysemanticity.

rows.subject: Gemma 3 27B
rows.operation_detail: Related concept-level measure: correlate mean granularity with best-found steering utility across concepts
rows.measure: Spearman correlation between concept granularity and best-found steering utility
rows.locator: Section 5.2, Granularity and the steering ceiling; Figure 4
rows.note: This is an association between a concept-level direction-heterogeneity statistic and steering utility, not a measurement of neuron polysemanticity.
rows.check: A concept-level granularity vs steering-utility correlation, not a neuron measure. The text gives ρ=−0.46 for Gemma 3 27B in Sec 5.2, but Appendix F reports the same ρ=−0.46 pooled over n=60 model–concept pairs, so the subject may be pooled rather than one model.

source_check.correct: Sec 5.2 says Figure 4 shows Gemma 3 27B (20 concepts), Spearman rho=-0.46, p=0.000. But Appendix D calls Figure 4 'the pooled comparison', and Appendix F gives the same rho=-0.46 (p=0.0002) pooled over n=60 model-concept pairs across all three models. p=0.000 fits n=60, not n=20.
source_check.locator_found: Sec 5.2 'Granularity and the steering ceiling'; Appendix D; Appendix F (Granularity vs steerability, n=60 pooled)
source_check.problem: The text contradicts itself: the value is credited to Gemma 3 27B in Sec 5.2 but looks pooled across three models (Appendix D/F).

rows.subject: Llama 3.3 70B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Related concept-level measure: correlate mean granularity with trials needed to reach 95% of best-found steering utility
rows.measure: Spearman correlation between concept granularity and T95
rows.locator: Section 5.2, Granularity and optimization difficulty; Figure 4
rows.note: T95 is a steering-search measure, not a neuron-response measure.
rows.check: A steering-search difficulty correlation (T95), not a neuron measure. The abstract gives Pearson r=0.44 for this relation, while the row records Spearman 0.37 for Llama 70B.

source_check.correct: Sec 5.2 credits rho=0.37 (p=0.003) to Llama 3.3 70B-Instruct, but Appendix D calls Figure 4 'the pooled comparison' across models. p=0.003 at rho=0.37 fits about 60 pooled model-concept pairs, not 20 concepts. The abstract gives Pearson r=0.44 (p<0.001) for this relation.

source_check.problem: Same contradiction as R1: credited to Llama 70B in Sec 5.2, but Appendix D says Figure 4 is pooled.
